findings.title: Validate every payment's tenant before processing the batch
findings.problem: The authorization check examines only `payments[0]`, but the loop refunds every returned payment. A later payment belonging to another tenant therefore bypasses tenant authorization.
findings.reason: `Payment.id` is documented as tenant-scoped, and `get_many` accepts only IDs without a tenant constraint. When a batch resolves to an authorized first payment followed by a captured payment from another tenant, the second payment reaches `record_refund`, allowing a cross-tenant refund. The check must cover the same set that is processed.
findings.suggestion: Validate `payment.tenant_id == actor.tenant_id` for every returned payment before recording any refund, preferably in a complete pre-validation pass so a bad item cannot leave a partially processed batch. Also constrain repository lookup by tenant where possible.

security.public_safe_summary: Validate every payment's tenant before processing the batch

findings.title: Keep the tenant in the repository idempotency key
findings.problem: The new repository key omits `actor.tenant_id` even though repository idempotency keys use a global namespace and payment IDs are unique only within a tenant.
findings.reason: Two tenants can submit the same caller idempotency key for payments with the same tenant-local ID, producing identical repository keys. The later refund can then collide with or be deduplicated against another tenant's operation, violating refund correctness and tenant isolation.
findings.suggestion: Restore a tenant-qualified key such as `f"{actor.tenant_id}:{idempotency_key}:{payment.id}"`, and add a test covering identical payment IDs and idempotency keys in different tenants.

security.public_safe_summary: Keep the tenant in the repository idempotency key

findings.title: Preserve the ID tie-breaker in pagination cursors
findings.problem: The cursor now encodes only `created_at`, discarding the payment ID even though query ordering is `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`.
findings.reason: When more than one row shares the boundary timestamp, the next request can only filter by time and cannot resume after the exact `(created_at, id)` tuple. Depending on the query's timestamp predicate, rows at that timestamp are skipped or repeated, so clients cannot reliably enumerate all payments.
findings.suggestion: Retain both `created_at` and `payment_id` in `Cursor`, pass the full cursor to `page_before`, and apply tuple/keyset pagination using both ordering columns. Add a multi-page test where several rows share the same timestamp.
